summary:
Bayelsa State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex unions and renders any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across Nigeria since 1916.

The maximum penalty a visitor faces in Bayelsa is 14 years' imprisonment. That is the southern ceiling under the secular national statute, and it applies to same-sex unions and same-sex sexual activity alike.

The death penalty does not reach Bayelsa. It is confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where penalties run from lashes or caning up to death by stoning; the UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025) states plainly that this risk does not extend to southern states such as Bayelsa.

No state-specific enforcement divergence for Bayelsa is documented in the sourced material. The same June 2025 note records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people, assessed as applying across all states, and those patterns therefore set the expectation for Bayelsa as much as for any other state.

The sources record no arrest, prosecution, mob attack or venue closure inside Bayelsa itself. Every documented enforcement incident in the inventory occurred in other Nigerian states, which means a visitor to Bayelsa is relying on a national assessment rather than on state-level evidence.
tangentialFactors:
Comparison across Nigerian states is the main turbulence signal. Recorded mass arrests at social venues include more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011. These figures rank states by raw counts only and track where raids were reported, not per-capita risk.

Bayelsa's contrast with the north is stark. A Shari'a court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning in 2022, a further death-by-stoning sentence from Bauchi was reported in May 2024, and in January 2014 a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial. None of that machinery exists in Bayelsa, where the secular 14-year framework governs.

Conditions documented elsewhere in Nigeria shape expectations in Bayelsa because the same statute and the same national police force operate throughout the country. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through dating apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, and TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a man stopped by Lagos police and struck in the mouth with a gun butt for 'looking gay'.

Whether a trans person held in custody would be placed according to gender identity remains unresolved nationally. Press coverage of Bobrisky's imprisonment in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, between 12 April and 5 August 2024 openly asked which prison would hold her, and an October 2024 panel found her maximum-security placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act; no parallel case or policy is sourced for Bayelsa.
localsOnly:
Bayelsa residents live under the same secular 14-year maximum as visitors, with no state sentencing divergence documented. The Shari'a penalties of the northern states, up to stoning, have no application to residents of Bayelsa.

No Bayelsa-specific instrument granting legal recognition of gender identity, anti-discrimination protection or recognition of same-sex relationships is documented in the sources. The absence is recorded as an absence of sourcing rather than as a finding of state law.

Residents have no documented state-level protection mechanism distinct from the national framework, and no Bayelsa enforcement statistic, prosecution record or police-command practice is available in the inventory. Countrywide findings on chilled access to healthcare and to reporting crimes to police apply to Bayelsa residents through the national assessment.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Bayelsa's own state criminal code contains offences beyond the 2014 national statute is unresolved; the sources address only the national Act as it applies in the state.

No Bayelsa-specific arrest, prosecution or sentencing data was located, so the state's enforcement level relative to Delta, Lagos or Gombe cannot be stated. Any comparison would rest on raw counts from other states.

The policing practice of the Bayelsa command, including how officers treat gender-nonconforming presentation during stops, is not sourced. Documented stop-and-extort cases come from Lagos only.

Whether Bayelsa operates any correctional placement policy for trans detainees, or any facility-access rule for trans visitors, is unresolved in the inventory.
